summary: Pointe-Sud-Ouest light, Anticosti's first (1831): stone tower, Pope family keepers, 1871 and 1874 wrecks, 1958 fire, top fell in 2011; the Coast Guard still lists a light.

light.note: Current light on a 1972 skeleton tower (Coast Guard list, entry 1515). The 1831 stone tower's light was discontinued in 1959.

structures.note: Tapered stone tower lined with fire brick inside (register). Register and LighthouseFriends give 22 m (72 ft); Route des phares and National Trust give 24 m. Top collapsed in August 2011.
Square skeleton tower with the current Fl W 6s light, year round. The register describes the steel open-frame structure (structure à claire-voie en acier).
Keeper's house burned in 1958; the station's other buildings were destroyed in 1984 (register). The Coast Guard demolished the keeper's quarters (National Trust).

access.note: Coast Guard property. Grounds open, tower closed (LighthouseFriends). Reached by four-wheel-drive vehicle on Anticosti; the last part is a rugged shore track of about 6 km.

events.note: John Lambly (Quebec harbour master) and Captain Bayfield, RN, recommend a light at this point (LighthouseFriends)
Stone tower built from 1830, under contract with W. Lander, two seasons (LighthouseFriends)
First shown 25 August 1831 (LighthouseFriends); the register dates first lighting to 1831 and calls it the first rotating light on the St. Lawrence
Lt. James Harvey, Royal Navy, first keeper (LighthouseFriends)
Edward Pope takes over as keeper; the Pope family keeps the light to 1899 (LighthouseFriends)
Tower clapboarded to keep out water (LighthouseFriends)
Revolving mechanism broke in August 1869 during a typhoid outbreak; the keeper turned the light by hand until it was replaced in June 1870 (LighthouseFriends)
Barque Russia rescue: keeper Pope and assistant William Nadean bring a boatswain ashore (LighthouseFriends)
Two horizontal red bands painted on the tower (LighthouseFriends). The register says the bands were original.
Zephirin Lemieux, keeper 1900 to 1924 (LighthouseFriends); named as keeper in the Department's table for the fiscal year ending March 1908
Single-flash long-focus reflector; characteristic changed to a 3.5 s flash and 3.5 s eclipse (LighthouseFriends)

Single-flash, long-focus reflector with 55 mm burner provided at Southwest point (Department table, FY ending March 1915; checked on the page image). LighthouseFriends dates a single-flash reflector to 1914.
Fire destroys the keeper's house and damages the tower; the register says the lantern and wooden cladding were lost
Stone tower's light discontinued after the 1958 fire; replaced by an automated light on an 80-foot tower (LighthouseFriends)
Fifty-foot skeleton tower, white flash every six seconds (LighthouseFriends; Coast Guard list)
All station buildings except the tower destroyed in 1984 (register)
Top of the tower collapses in August 2011 (National Trust; LighthouseFriends says around August 2011)

wrecks.outcome: Foundered in a winter gale; one crewman drowned, boatswain rescued by keeper Pope and assistant; crew wintered at the light (LighthouseFriends). The British ship register gives 10 May 1872 with one crew member lost.

Struck the reefs with sixteen men aboard; six lost in the surf, the captain and seven froze in the rigging; two survivors sheltered by the Popes until spring (LighthouseFriends; Société historique du Golfe headstone)
Went ashore on Anticosti near South West Point; formal inquiry at Quebec (Department's wreck list)
Ran ashore; the salvage list places her off South West Point (salved 23-30 Aug), the wreck inquiry at Bagot Bluff on 22 Aug. The two records disagree.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The Coast Guard list (entry 1515) still gives a year-round light, so 'active' matches it. The National Trust for Canada says the light has been out of use since the early 1990s and the Route des phares calls the site decommissioned and threatened. The sources conflict; not resolved here.
Tower height: 22 m (72 ft) per the register and LighthouseFriends; 24 m per the National Trust and Route des phares. Not resolved.
Russia: LighthouseFriends dates the loss to 6 December 1871; the vessel record gives 10 May 1872 with one crew member lost. Not resolved.
Admiral Hastings (1919): the Quebec Salvage and Wrecking Company list places her off South West point (salved 23-30 August); the wreck inquiry places her on Bagot Bluff on 22 August. Not resolved.
Paint: the register says the tower was built white with two wide horizontal red bands; LighthouseFriends says the bands were painted on in 1881. Not resolved.

notes_for_editor: 1) Keepers: LighthouseFriends is the only full keeper list. The keeper table for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1908 (Appendix No. 12, scan p. 192) was checked on the page image: the 'south west point' row carries Z. Lemieux (appointed 10 July 1900, salary $700) and the 'west point' row carries Alf. Malouin. The match is by row on the image, not by OCR column order. 2) The 1915 Quebec table (scan p. 55, printed p. 48) was checked on the page image. The Southwest point row carries only the provision and installation of a single-flash, long-focus reflector with a 55 mm burner. The 'Erection of new dwelling to replace one destroyed by fire' belongs to the Stone Pillar row (contract, J. E. Fortin, St. Jean, Port Joli, P.Q.), so the earlier draft's dwelling and fire claims for Southwest point are removed. 3) The reflector: LighthouseFriends dates a single-flash, long-focus reflector to 1914; the table's entry falls in the fiscal year April 1914 to March 1915. The sources do not say they are the same installation. 4) The 1902 and 1903 meteorological observers were checked in the corpus text (scans 191 and 116, printed pp. 14 and 103); the reports do not say whether the observer was the keeper Zephirin Lemieux. 5) Russia wreck: LighthouseFriends dates it 6 December 1871; the vessel record gives 10 May 1872 with one crew member lost. Unresolved. 6) Admiral Hastings (1919): the salvage list says off South West point; the wreck inquiry says Bagot Bluff on 22 August, and prints the name 'Admiral Hasting'. Unresolved. 7) Tower height: 22 m (register, LighthouseFriends) vs 24 m (Route des phares, National Trust). Unresolved. 8) Status: the Coast Guard list says year round; the National Trust and Route des phares say disused. The record's 'status: active' is consistent with the Coast Guard list only. 9) The 1900 Chief Engineer's report (scan p. 56, printed p. 41): the telegraph house about 600 feet from the lighthouse and the acre surveyed round the lighthouse are in the Southwest point entry; the 'Mr. Menier's surveyor' remark is applied to Southwest point in the same report. 10) Record's visit.boat_only is true; LighthouseFriends describes a four-wheel-drive route and a 6 km shore track on Anticosti, and its writer's visit took most of a day. Check before publishing. 11) Trinity House's choice of site is given by the register only; Trinity House's own records were not read. 12) Sauver Duguay and Roger Poulin appear in LighthouseFriends with no dates. Keeper Evariste Ferguson is spelled as LighthouseFriends prints it; a tourism page spells the name Évariste, not checked. 13) LighthouseFriends is copyrighted: the story paraphrases it and quotes it at most in a phrase. 14) No photos sourced.
